hero.title: Amending Act of 1786
hero.description: Passed specifically to accommodate the demands of Lord Cornwallis, this Act marked a critical step in the concentration of executive and military authority in the Governor-General.

cards.details: Established the office of Governor-General of Bengal, subordinate to a four-member council, creating executive vulnerability.
Resolved the jurisdiction clash between the Supreme Court and the Governor-General-in-Council.

mnemonics.title: Mnemonics & Memory Hacks
mnemonics.description: Use these visual memory hooks to retain critical facts about the Amending Act of 1786 for the UPSC Civil Services Examination.

items.title: Mnemonic 1: Cornwallis's Demands
items.decryption: Remember the two conditions of **C**ornwallis: **C**ouncil override power, and becoming the **C**ommander-in-Chief.

items.title: Mnemonic 2: Scope of Override
items.phrase: "S-P-I (Override only for Safety, Peace, or Interests)"
items.decryption: The Governor-General could not override the Council in daily routine matters, but only on matters affecting the **S**afety, **P**eace, or **I**nterests of the British Empire in India.

flashcards.title: Active Recall Flashcards
flashcards.description: Use these active recall questions to reinforce fact-dense syllabus details on the Amending Act of 1786.

items.question: For whose appointment was the Amending Act of 1786 specifically enacted?
items.answer: It was enacted to satisfy the preconditions of Lord Cornwallis before he accepted the post of Governor-General of Bengal.

items.question: What was the first major concession granted to Lord Cornwallis by this Act?
items.answer: The power to override the decision of his Council in special cases, acting on his own responsibility.

items.question: What was the second major concession granted to Lord Cornwallis by this Act?
items.answer: He was appointed as the Commander-in-Chief of the British forces in India, combining military and executive heads.

items.question: Could the Governor-General override the council on ordinary commercial matters?
items.answer: No. The overriding power was restricted to extraordinary situations involving the safety, peace, or interests of the presidency.

items.question: Which subsequent Act extended these overriding powers to all future Governor-Generals?
items.answer: The Charter Act of 1793 generalized this overriding power for all future Governor-Generals and Presidency Governors.

traps.title: UPSC Prelims Traps to Avoid
items: Trap 1: Do not assume that the overriding power was a permanent feature of the Regulating Act of 1773 or Pitt's India Act of 1784. It was introduced solely in 1786 as an amendment.

Trap 2: The Act did not abolish the Governor-General's Council. The Council remained, and the Governor-General had to consult them, but he could override their majority opinion in special cases, bearing personal responsibility.

Trap 3: The Commander-in-Chief office was not permanently combined with the Governor-Generalship for all times. The Act allowed them to be combined, and Lord Cornwallis held both, but they remained separate offices that could be united if the Crown/Company chose.
Trap 4: The override power did not apply to judicial functions. The Governor-General-in-Council still acted as the Sadar Diwani Adalat, where normal legal protocols applied.

deepDive.title: Syllabus Core Study Notes (Deep-Dive)
deepDive.description: Master the historical context, statutory modifications, and long-term constitutional impacts of the Amending Act of 1786.

sections.title: 1. Genesis of the Act: Lord Cornwallis's Preconditions
sections.content:
Following the resignation of Warren Hastings and the implementation of Pitt's India Act of 1784, the British government faced significant administrative hurdles in consolidating its holdings in India. To execute crucial land revenue reforms and confront military threats like Tipu Sultan of Mysore, the British Cabinet selected Lord Cornwallis, a highly respected military general and nobleman. However, Cornwallis refused to accept the Governor-Generalship unless granted supreme authority.

Cornwallis's Demands for Acceptance

Cornwallis was determined to avoid the administrative paralysis that Warren Hastings had faced due to constant conflict with his Council members (who frequently outvoted him). He insisted on two non-negotiable preconditions:

  • Veto Power over Council: The statutory authority to override the majority decision of his Council in special situations, allowing him to act on his own personal responsibility.
  • Unified Military Command: The consolidation of the civil executive head (Governor-General) and the military head (Commander-in-Chief) into one office.
Administrative Rationale

The British Cabinet under Prime Minister William Pitt and the Board of Control President Henry Dundas accepted these demands. They recognized that the executive head in India required absolute, undivided authority to execute reforms (which later culminated in the Permanent Settlement of Bengal in 1793) and secure British territories. Parliament passed the Amending Act of 1786 specifically to enact these changes.

Concentration of Power Structure (1786 onwards)

sections.title: 2. Statutory Provisions & Constitutional Impact
sections.content:
The Act achieved its objectives through two primary statutory clauses, fundamentally altering the operational dynamics of the East India Company's supreme government in Bengal.

The Override Provision

The Act enabled the Governor-General to override the majority decision of the Council in cases where he judged the safety, peace, or interests of the British possessions in India were essentially concerned. In such cases, the Governor-General had to personally sign the order, taking full responsibility for the measures taken without Council concurrence.

Long-term Constitutional Legacy

This Act marked the transition from a **collaborative council government** to a **strong executive presidency** system. It established a precedent of vesting absolute power in a single executive head during crises. This pattern of concentrated authority was extended to future Governor-Generals via the Charter Act of 1793 and survived throughout British rule, influencing the strong executive model in post-independence India.

Constitutional Comparison: Pitt's India Act (1784) vs. Amending Act of 1786

Feature Pitt's India Act of 1784 Amending Act of 1786
Executive Council Power Decisions by majority vote. GG had only a casting vote in case of ties. GG was granted overriding veto power over the Council in special cases.
Military Command Commander-in-Chief was a separate office, usually held by a different general. The office of Commander-in-Chief was combined with the Governor-Generalship.
Administrative Philosophy Collective cabinet responsibility with reduced Council size (3 members). Concentration of absolute executive and military authority in the Governor-General.
